stemMd:
> From next year every law firm in the city must publish its fee schedule online. Since clients will then be able to compare fees before choosing a firm, the average fees charged by the city's law firms will fall.

The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Publishing a fee schedule online costs a law firm very little.

options.label: B
options.textMd: All the city's law firms currently charge roughly the same fees.

options.label: C
options.textMd: At least some clients choose a law firm partly on the basis of its fees.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Every client will choose the cheapest firm that is available.

explanationMd:
An assumption is an unstated premise the argument cannot do without. Find the gap between the evidence and the conclusion.

The argument moves from "clients **can** compare fees" to "fees **will** fall". That step works only if comparing fees affects which firm clients choose — otherwise firms would have no reason to lower their prices. So the argument needs at least some clients to choose a firm partly on the basis of its fees.

**How to check — the negation test.** Deny the statement: *no client takes fees into account at all when choosing a firm.* Then the published schedules would change nobody's choice, firms would lose no clients by keeping their prices, and the predicted fall in fees has no support. Because denying it destroys the argument, it is an assumption the argument depends on.

distractorRationale.b: The argument does not need this, and it would actually work against it: if all firms already charged the same, comparing schedules would reveal no cheaper option to switch to. The argument relies on fees differing.
distractorRationale.a: The cost of publishing is irrelevant to whether comparison will push fees down. Even if publishing were expensive, the argument's reasoning about client choice would be unaffected.
distractorRationale.d: This is far stronger than the argument needs. Fees can fall if only some clients are influenced by price; denying that every client picks the cheapest firm leaves the argument standing.

accessibilityText: An assumption question. The argument says that from next year every law firm in the city must publish its fee schedule online, and that, since clients will then be able to compare fees before choosing a firm, the average fees charged by the city's law firms will fall. The question asks which assumption the argument depends on. The four answer options are: publishing a fee schedule online costs a law firm very little; all the city's law firms currently charge roughly the same fees; at least some clients choose a law firm partly on the basis of its fees; every client will choose the cheapest firm that is available.

provenance.notes: Original assumption item with a necessary assumption, a too-strong version of it, an irrelevant cost premise and a premise that would undercut the argument. The city rule is invented.

review.author: bocconi-law-wave8-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Negation test: if no client chooses a firm partly on fees, comparing fees would put no pressure on prices and the conclusion collapses. 'Every client chooses the cheapest firm' is sufficient but not necessary. Negating the low cost of publishing or the claim that firms charge similar fees does not break the argument; if anything, varied fees help it. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-final-verbal-run1) reached the same answer: Negation test: if no client chooses a firm even partly on fees, being able to compare fees creates no price pressure and the argument collapses. 'Every client picks the cheapest firm' is sufficient but too strong, so it is not required. A low cost of publishing and current similar fees are not needed; similar fees would, if anything, undercut the argument.]
